t:
(a) 
Section 10901(a) of title 49, United States Code, is amended by striking “will be enhanced by” and inserting in lieu thereof “permit”.
 
    (b) 
Section 10901 of title 49, United States Code, is further amended by adding at the end thereof the following new subsections:


“(d)

(1) 
Where a rail carrier has been issued a certificate of public convenience and necessity by the Commission authorizing the construction or extension of a railroad line, no other rail carrier may block such construction or extension by refusing to permit the carrier to cross its property if (A) the construction does not unreasonably interfere with the operation of the crossed line, (B) the operation does not materially interfere with the operation of the crossed line, and (C) the owner of the crossing line compensates the owner of the crossed line.


“(2) 
If the carriers are unable to agree on the terms of operation or the amount of payment for purposes of paragraph (1) of this subsection, either party may submit the matters in dispute to the Commission for determination.



“(e) 
The Commission may require any rail carrier proposing both to construct and operate a new railroad line pursuant to this section to provide a fair and equitable arrangement for the protection of the interests of railroad employees who may be affected thereby no less protective of and beneficial to the interests of such employees than those established pursuant to section 11347 of this title.”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that rail carriers (outside parties) bringing a dispute to the Commission counts as participation. But this is agency adjudication of a private dispute between two carriers over crossing terms and compensation, not consultation with outsiders before a federal policy decision, and it grants no right to sue or object to a federal decision. The rest of the section concerns certificates (license applications) and employee-protection conditions the Commission may impose, with no comment period, hearing, advisory body, or required rulemaking.
fable.s: either party may submit the matters in dispute to the Commission for determination

opus.w: The only outside-party involvement is that private rail carriers can ask the Commission to settle a two-party dispute over crossing terms and compensation. That is a way to resolve a dispute, like an appeal or application. It is not consulting outsiders before a federal policy decision. Nothing in the section creates a comment period, public hearing, advisory body, rulemaking requirement, or right to sue over a federal decision. Subsection (e) only gives the Commission authority to impose employee-protection conditions.
opus.s: If the carriers are unable to agree on the terms of operation or the amount of payment for purposes of paragraph (1) of this subsection, either party may submit the matters in dispute to the Commission for determination.
opus.b: 1. **Tempting reading:** Subsection (d)(2) lets rail carriers, which are private parties outside the federal government, "submit the matters in dispute to the Commission for determination." That looks like outsiders taking part in a federal decision. It isn't participation as defined. This is a way to have the agency settle a private business dispute (crossing terms and payment). It is not consulting outsiders before a policy decision. That makes it closer to the appeal-like exchange in Example 11 or to an application. Subsection (e) only lets the Commission impose employee-protection conditions. It requires no consultation, hearing, comment period or rulemaking.

qwen_chat.w: This section describes a dispute resolution mechanism where rail carriers submit disagreements to the Commission for determination. This is an adjudicative or regulatory enforcement process, not a consultation or coordination process where the government seeks input from outside parties before making a decision. The definition of participation requires the government to consult or coordinate with outsiders (like states, tribes, public, experts) before making a decision, often via advisory boards or comment periods. Resolving a dispute between two private parties after they have failed to agree is not 'participation' in the defined sense. Additionally, the employee protection clause mandates the carrier to provide protection, with Commission oversight, rather than requiring the Commission to consult with employees.
qwen_chat.s: If the carriers are unable to agree on the terms of operation or the amount of payment for purposes of paragraph (1) of this subsection, either party may submit the matters in dispute to the Commission for determination.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement for the Commission to determine disputes between rail carriers or to require arrangements for employee protection constitutes participation because it involves outside parties (carriers, employees) interacting with a federal agency. However, this interaction is part of a regulatory enforcement or adjudicative process regarding specific operational disputes or labor protections, not a consultation or coordination process where the government seeks input from outsiders *before* making a broader policy decision. The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits/licenses and focuses on consultation/coordination/advisory roles. The dispute resolution mechanism is a standard administrative adjudication, not "participation" in the sense of bringing outsiders into the decision-making loop via consultation or advisory boards. Furthermore, the employee protection clause is a mandate for the carrier to provide protection, with the Commission having oversight authority, not a requirement for the Commission to consult with employees.
